data_quality_assurance: Data quality assurance will be ensured through multiple quality control steps implemented during data generation and bioinformatic processing. Raw sequencing data quality will be evaluated using standard sequencing metrics and preprocessing tools such as fastp for read filtering and trimming. Alignment statistics, coverage metrics, and classification outputs will be examined to verify data integrity and consistency. Intermediate results will be inspected to identify potential technical artefacts, and datasets will be checked for completeness and consistency before deposition and further analysis.
dataset.description: The following section outlines the research data management strategy for the SPERMFREE project. It describes the types of data generated during the project, including next-generation sequencing data from seminal plasma cell-free DNA, derived bioinformatic datasets, and associated pseudonymized clinical metadata. The plan defines how these data will be processed, stored, protected, and preserved throughout the project lifecycle using institutional research infrastructures, including the RTU High Performance Computing (HPC) environment for large-scale genomic data processing and the RSU Dataverse repository for long-term archiving of curated datasets. The approach ensures compliance with FAIR data principles while protecting sensitive patient information and intellectual property related to the analytical workflow developed in the project.

distribution.title:
The data generated in the SPERMFREE project aim to investigate molecular signatures of spermatogenic activity and inflammation in men with severe male infertility using cell-free DNA (cfDNA) derived from seminal plasma. The collected data support the development and validation of an integrated analytical workflow that combines multiple cfDNA-derived features, including fragmentation patterns, inferred gene expression signals, mitochondrial DNA coverage, and microbial signatures, to provide a non-invasive assessment of testicular function.

The primary data originate from seminal plasma samples collected from patients undergoing clinical evaluation for infertility in collaborating fertility clinics. From these samples, cfDNA will be extracted and sequenced using next-generation sequencing (NGS) technologies. Subsequent bioinformatic analyses will generate derived datasets describing genomic fragmentation profiles, sequence motif patterns, microbial taxonomic composition, and gene-level fragmentation metrics. These molecular data will be integrated with pseudonymized clinical parameters, such as spermogram results and patient characteristics, to develop and validate the SPERMFREE analytical framework.

This data generation directly supports the project objective of establishing a reproducible and interpretable molecular workflow for assessing spermatogenic activity and inflammation-related dysfunction in severe male infertility.

security_and_privacy.description: Research data are stored within secure institutional infrastructures used by the project, including the RTU High-Performance Computing environment for sequencing data processing and RSU institutional systems for documentation and curated datasets. Access to the data is restricted to authorized project researchers and controlled through institutional authentication systems. Data processing and analysis are conducted on RTU high-performance computing infrastructure with user-level access control. Data are stored on institutional servers with regular backup procedures and maintained according to RSU IT security and research data management policies. Any datasets containing sensitive information are handled in accordance with applicable data protection regulations and institutional ethical approvals.

dmp.description:
The Data Management Plan (DMP) describes how research data generated within the SPERMFREE project will be collected, processed, stored, protected, and preserved throughout the project lifecycle. The project will generate several types of data, including next-generation sequencing (NGS) data from seminal plasma cell-free DNA, derived bioinformatic datasets (e.g., fragmentomic profiles, microbial signatures, and inferred gene-expression features), and associated pseudonymized clinical metadata.

Raw sequencing data and intermediate computational files will be processed and temporarily stored using the High-Performance Computing (HPC) infrastructure provided by the Riga Technical University (RTU) High-Performance Computing Center. This infrastructure supports large-scale genomic data processing and secure storage required for next-generation sequencing analyses.

Curated datasets supporting scientific analyses and publications will be archived in the institutional RSU Dataverse repository to ensure long-term preservation and compliance with FAIR data principles. Sensitive patient-related information will remain pseudonymized and stored in secure institutional systems.

The bioinformatic workflow developed in this project constitutes a potentially patentable analytical technology; therefore, the pipeline source code will be maintained in a private version-controlled repository accessible only to the project team. Public release of proprietary components will be considered after completion of intellectual property protection procedures.
dmp.ethical_issues_description: Yes. The study involves analysis of human-derived biological material and genomic sequencing data, which may contain sensitive information. All samples are processed in accordance with approved ethical protocols and institutional regulations governing research involving human biological material. Personal identifiers are removed or replaced with pseudonymized identifiers prior to data processing to ensure participant confidentiality. In addition, certain analytical methods developed within the project may be subject to intellectual property protection, which may influence the extent to which some technical details or intermediate analysis components are publicly shared. Data sharing will therefore follow applicable ethical approvals, institutional data protection policies, and intellectual property considerations.
